NP-complete problems. The hardest problems in NP. They are both in NP, meaning they are verifiable in polynomial time, and they are NP-hard, meaning they are at least as hard as every other problem in NP. The existence of a polynomial-time algorithm for any NP-complete problem would prove P equals NP and would revolutionize mathematics and cryptography. A problem is NP-complete if it is in NP and NP-hard. Every other NP problem can be reduced to it in polynomial time. The first NP-complete problem was Boolean Satisfiability, or SAT, proved by Stephen Cook in 1971. Thousands of NP-complete problems are now known. Famous examples include the Travelling Salesman Problem, the Clique Problem, Vertex Cover, Hamiltonian Cycle, three-SAT, and Integer Knapsack. All known NP-complete problems have exponential-time algorithms. None are known to be in P, but none are proven to be outside it. If P does not equal NP, which is conjectured, then NP-complete problems are strictly harder than polynomial-time solvable ones and have no fast general solution. NP-complete problems have significant practical importance. They underpin the hardness assumptions for modern cryptography, such as the assumptions about integer factorization. To prove a new problem is NP-complete, use the reduction technique: show it is in NP and that SAT or another known NP-complete problem reduces to it. NP-complete problems are a subset of NP, while NP-hard problems need not be in NP. NP-complete equals the intersection of NP-hard and NP. If any NP-complete problem is in P, then P equals NP. NP-complete problems are decision problems by definition.
